summary: Genesis 24 tells how a wife is found for Isaac. Abraham, "old, and well stricken in age," makes his eldest servant swear not to take a Canaanite wife for his son but to go to Abraham's own country and kindred, trusting that God "shall send his angel before thee." The servant travels to Mesopotamia and stops at a well, praying for a clear sign: the girl who offers water both to him and to his camels will be the one appointed for Isaac. Before he finishes speaking, Rebekah appears, and she does exactly as he prayed—"Drink, and I will give thy camels drink also." The servant, "wondering at her," learns she is of Abraham's own family, and "bowed down his head, and worshipped the LORD." Received into the household of Bethuel and Laban, he refuses to eat until he has told his errand, recounting the whole story. Laban and Bethuel acknowledge, "The thing proceedeth from the LORD," and Rebekah freely consents: "I will go." She is blessed to become "the mother of thousands of millions." Journeying back, she meets Isaac as he "went out to meditate in the field at the eventide." Isaac brings her into Sarah's tent, and "she became his wife; and he loved her: and Isaac was comforted after his mother's death."
takeaways: The servant models prayerful dependence: he asks God for guidance, watches for the answer, and worships at once when it comes, giving God the credit for a "prosperous" journey.
Rebekah's generosity to a stranger and his thirsty camels reveals her character; the sign the servant sought was not a random omen but a test of kindness and diligence.
God's providence works through ordinary means—a journey, a well, a hospitable girl—so that human choices and divine guidance meet, and Rebekah's free "I will go" matters.
The chapter closes with love and comfort: Isaac loves Rebekah, and the sorrow over Sarah's death gives way to consolation, showing God's care threading through grief.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 28:1-2 — Isaac charges Jacob to take a wife from kindred, not Canaan
crossRefs.why: The same concern to marry within the covenant family, refusing Canaanite wives, is passed down to the next generation. Isaac sends Jacob back to the very household this chapter drew Rebekah from, showing a deliberate covenant marriage pattern.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 29:9-12 — Jacob meets Rachel at the well
crossRefs.why: The betrothal-at-a-well scene recurs when Jacob meets Rachel, echoing his mother Rebekah's story. The repeated well motif marks providential meetings that lead to covenant marriages.

crossRefs.label: John 4:6-14 — Jesus meets the Samaritan woman at a well
crossRefs.why: The Gospel scene of a meeting at a well, with a request for water that opens into deeper significance, resonates with the patriarchal well-betrothals. Christian readers see Jesus, the true Bridegroom, seeking his own at the well and offering living water.

crossRefs.label: Proverbs 19:14 — "a prudent wife is from the LORD"
crossRefs.why: The wisdom saying that a good wife is a gift of the LORD crystallizes the theology of this whole chapter: the right spouse is not merely found by effort but given by God, confirmed by Laban's own words that "the thing proceedeth from the LORD."

interpretationNotes.claim: A long Christian allegorical tradition, embraced in Catholic reading, sees the marriage of Isaac as a figure of Christ and the Church: Abraham the father sends the servant (often read as a figure of the Holy Spirit or of gospel messengers) to seek a bride for the beloved son, adorning her with gifts and leading her home. Rebekah's veiling and free consent are read as the Church's response to the Bridegroom.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the chapter first as a historical account of covenant faithfulness and God's guiding providence in ordinary life, and many are cautious about mapping each figure onto a fixed allegory. Where the bridegroom-and-bride imagery of Christ and the Church is affirmed, it is usually grounded in the New Testament's explicit use of that image rather than pressed from the narrative details here.
